newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures settled near a new contract high on Thursday, supported by a U.S. market that drew inspiration from bond-friendly jobs data which stirred hope that a slight slowdown in the American economy was underway.

"The French market is benefiting from a strong international outlook with the strength of the T-bond, accentuated without a doubt by short buying ahead of the three-day U.S. holiday weekend," said market economist Joanne Perez of Merrill Lynch.
After starting out the day in negative territory, the September 10-year bond future turned positive on the back of the data.

The notionnel finished up 22 basis points at 129.88, close to the new contract high of 129.92 set after the U.S. employment figures signalled a slowdown from the heady economic pace set in the first quarter and made an August rate hike seem less likely.
The U.S. June unemployment rate rose to 5.0 percent from 4.8 percent. June non-farm payrolls rose 217,000 against a forecast 222,000.
"Leaving aside the international environment, we are also benefiting from an injection of liquidity from the Balladur bond," said Credit Agricole Indosuez chief market economist Stuart Thomson.

The 1993 bond was issued by conservative former prime minister Edouard Balladur to fund an economic recovery plan and some of the 91 billion francs to be returned to investors on July 16 is expected to find its way to the bond market.

Thomson said there was buying at the shorter end, especially in the five year zone. He said investors were more negative toward longer-dated maturities amid expectations yields would rise to six percent at the 10-year end in the second half.
The market was unfazed by the new Socialist government's warning the public deficit was likely to significantly overshoot criteria set in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.

"At the moment, the deficit is not a concern," Thomson said. "There is a feeling that whatever figures may come out in the short-term, the government will do what is necessary to qualify for monetary union."
He said that France was expected to reduce the 1997 deficit to 3.3 percent or possibly 3.2 percent of gross domestic product.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday the deficit could be significantly higher than forecast this year but that the government would take action if needed to curb it.

Strauss-Kahn suggested, however, that the government would not take radical measures to cut the deficit to precisely 3.0 percent of GDP, the target fixed by its main partner Germany to qualify for the single currency.
The previous centre right government had targeted deficit/GDP ratio of 3.0 percent.
The market was expected to be calm on Friday with the U.S. market closed for the Independence Day holiday.
September PIBOR was quiet, finishing unchanged at 96.57.
